Command
kom-mänd'
v.t. and n. (to order with authority; rendering Hebrew tsavah, Greek entellomai)
From Latin com, with, and mandare, to commit or enjoin. Hebrew tsavah is to lay a charge upon someone, and its noun mitzvah is a commandment — the standing word for what God has enjoined and for what a father enjoins his household.

Biblical Definition

Command is to lay a charge with authority, and Scripture uses the word of God, of Moses, and of parents, in that descending order of derivation. God's commanding is not arbitrary and, Moses insists, not obscure: “For this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off” (Deuteronomy 30:11). Nor may it be adjusted: “What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deuteronomy 12:32). Human commands derive from and are limited by it. Rebekah's charge to Jacob — “obey my voice according to that which I command thee” (Genesis 27:8) — is a mother using rightful authority to procure a deception, and the family never recovers. The Pharisees press Christ on the divorce certificate: “Why did Moses then command to give a writing of divorcement?” (Matthew 19:7), and His answer distinguishes what Moses suffered for hardness of heart from what was commanded from the beginning. And Christ leaves His own commandment, which is love (John 15:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

To order or enjoin with authority; and the charge so given. In Scripture God's commandment is neither hidden nor far off, and may be neither added to nor diminished; human authority to command is derived from His and bounded by it.

expand to see more

COMMAND, v.t. [L. com and mando, to commit, to enjoin.] To bid; to order; to direct with authority.

2. To govern; to lead; to have under direction or control.

3. COMMAND, n. The right or power of governing with chief authority; an order given.

4. COMMANDMENT, n. A command; a mandate; a precept of the divine law.

5. In Scripture, this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not hidden from thee, Deut. 30; This is my commandment, John 15.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 30:11 — "For this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off."

Deuteronomy 12:32 — "What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it."

Genesis 27:8 — "Now therefore, my son, obey my voice according to that which I command thee."

John 15:12 — "This is my commandment, That ye love one another, as I have loved you."

Modern Corruption

Two errors attend the word: the claim that God's commands are too obscure to be obeyed, and the treatment of derived human authority — parental, ecclesiastical, civil — as though it were absolute rather than answerable.

expand to see more

Moses forecloses the first in advance. The commandment is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off; it is not in heaven, nor beyond the sea, but very nigh, in the mouth and in the heart. Where Scripture is genuinely difficult the difficulty is real, and the Confession acknowledges that not all things are alike plain; but it insists that those things necessary to be known, believed, and observed for salvation are so clearly propounded that the unlearned may attain a sufficient understanding of them. An appeal to obscurity is very often an evasion, and the words a man understands are usually the ones he most wishes he did not.

The second error is the more dangerous because it wears the language of obedience. Rebekah commanded Jacob, and had a mother's right to command, and used it to procure a lie; Jacob obeyed and spent twenty years in exile for it. All human authority is derived, and therefore bounded: the apostles answered the council that we ought to obey God rather than men, and Scripture nowhere requires submission to a command that God forbids. Parents, elders, and magistrates all rule under a Lawgiver, and the man who commands must answer for the command as surely as the man who obeys must answer for the obedience.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsavah is to lay a charge upon, and its noun mitzvah is a commandment; Greek entellomai is to enjoin, and entole is the commandment, the word in this is my commandment.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsavah (H6680) — to lay a charge upon, to command, to appoint; used of God, of Moses, and of parents.

Hebrew mitzvah (H4687) — a commandment; the standing noun for a precept of the divine law.

Greek entellomai (G1781) — to enjoin, to give charge; the verb behind the Great Commission's all things whatsoever I have commanded you.

Greek entole (G1785) — a commandment; the noun in This is my commandment, That ye love one another.

Latin mandare — to commit, to enjoin; the root of command and of mandate.

Usage

"Of a commandment neither hidden nor distant: it is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off (Deuteronomy 30:11)."

"Of a law that may be neither supplemented nor reduced: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it (Deuteronomy 12:32)."

"Of Christ's own commandment to His disciples: This is my commandment, That ye love one another (John 15:12)."
